subject: Computer Networking
title: DNS: Names to Numbers
description: A quick win: understand DNS: Names to Numbers.

hook.text: Humans remember names. Computers need numbers. DNS bridges the gap every time you visit a site.

buildup.text: DNS is hierarchical: root servers at the top, then TLD servers (.com, .org), then authoritative name servers.

discovery.text: A full lookup walks down the tree: root → .com → example.com → IP address. Each step narrows the search.

twist.text: Results are cached aggressively. Your device, router, and ISP all remember recent answers to save time.

climax.text: DNS was designed without encryption. DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS now protect your queries from snooping.

punchline.text: DNS translates names to IPs so you never have to.

details.summary: DNS translates human-readable domain names like example.com into IP addresses that computers use to route traffic. The hierarchical system of root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative name servers resolves billions of queries daily, with caching at every level for speed.
details.whyItMatters: DNS is the first step of almost every internet interaction. A DNS failure or slowdown makes the entire internet appear broken, even when servers are perfectly healthy.
takeaways: DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses hierarchically
Recursive resolvers cache answers to speed up repeated queries
TTL values control how long DNS answers are cached

faq.question: What happens during a DNS lookup?
faq.answer: Your device asks a recursive resolver, which checks its cache. If not cached, it queries a root server for the TLD server, then the TLD server for the authoritative name server, then the authoritative server for the IP address. Each answer is cached per its TTL value.

faq.question: What is a DNS TTL value?
faq.answer: Time-to-live tells resolvers how long to cache a DNS answer in seconds. A short TTL like 60 seconds allows fast changes but increases query load. A long TTL like 86400 seconds reduces load but delays propagation of changes. Most sites use TTLs between 300 and 3600 seconds.
